source.title: Beyond In-Distribution Success: Scaling Curves of CoT Granularity for Language Model Generalization
source.authors: Ru Wang; Wei Huang; Selena Song; Hao-Yu Zhang; Qian Niu; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo; Jia-Xian Guo

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures task accuracy as training dataset size changes, a different measure and setting from the original held-out-loss scaling laws. This bears on V6, but it does not test power-law loss scaling or fit the original laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports dataset-size accuracy curves for synthetic compound tasks, so those results bear on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, vary parameter count or compute, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The recap-condition ablation and CoT-granularity comparisons are not rows because they do not measure scaling with dataset size.
record.test_reason: The study measures how OOD compound-task accuracy changes with training-data scale in a new synthetic setting. These results bear on V6's improvement-with-scale component, although the study fits no predictive law and measures no pretraining loss. Training-set accuracy does not establish downstream predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase accurately summarizes the data-scaling conclusion. The authors also conclude that finer-grained CoT improves OOD generalization and sample efficiency, and argue that explicit reasoning paths and subtask recaps explain these benefits. They acknowledge synthetic-task scope, increased inference costs from longer CoT, and no empirical verification on 100B+ parameter models.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses synthetic compound-task accuracy and varies training dataset size and CoT supervision; it does not use the original studies’ held-out pretraining-loss measurement, parameter/compute sweeps, or power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: OOD accuracy trends depend on CoT supervision ratio: 70–100% CoT is described as improving with scale, direct Q-A as plateauing, and partial CoT as degrading OOD performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-set accuracy improves or remains high as the task-training dataset grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing task-training data can yield high training accuracy without ensuring OOD generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Partial CoT supervision has lower OOD accuracy than more complete CoT supervision; the text does not establish the individual partial-CoT scaling slopes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CoT step coverage affects OOD compound-task accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: Third Conference on Parsimony and Learning (CPAL 2026)
record.problems: Scaling-curve values are presented as plots without numeric per-size results or uncertainty estimates in the text. The methods state dataset sizes from 1k to 30k, while the scaling figure axis and accompanying prose extend to 10000k samples. The experiments use synthetic compound tasks and do not establish a power-law fit.
record.rows_left_out: No additional dataset-size scaling results are stated outside the MPC and LIS curves in Figure 5; no rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss, its power-law form, and scaling with parameters, tokens or compute.
Predicting larger-run losses from fits to smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its scaling exponents.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes; task-specific training alone does not test this form.

Quantitative predictive fits or extrapolation, relationships with pretraining loss, parameter or compute scaling, and broad downstream benchmarks. The tested component is qualitative OOD accuracy improvement with task-training dataset size.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices. Accuracy plateaus alone do not establish bending of a fitted loss power law.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains figure axes and captions but no readable plotted traces, so individual trajectories cannot be independently digitized. CoT percentages represent retained reasoning-step coverage rather than clearly defined fractions of CoT examples; the methods inconsistently call them dropout rates. QA evaluation scores the final answer, whereas CoT evaluation also incorporates intermediate computational tokens, limiting direct accuracy comparisons across supervision conditions. Neither this measurement difference nor annotation quality dependence alone tests V7. No files or external sources were accessed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Prediction of larger-run losses from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.

The paper varies training dataset size rather than model parameter count or pretraining loss; it does not fit a predictive scaling law. It tests task accuracy on synthetic compound tasks, not broad downstream benchmark performance.
The paper does not compare scaling-law fitting choices, exponents, or compute-optimal splits, and does not analyze departures from a single power law.

relationships.condition: MPC and LIS OOD evaluation with 70–100% CoT supervision as training datasets grow
relationships.reason: Sections 4.2.1–4.2.4 explicitly describe continuing OOD gains with scale for high-CoT models, supporting qualitative improvement in r9, r10, r19 and r20; no quantitative prediction law is validated.
relationships.display_finding: Models with 70–100% chain-of-thought supervision continue improving on out-of-distribution MPC and LIS evaluations as training data increases, without a validated quantitative prediction law.

relationships.condition: MPC and LIS OOD evaluation with direct QA supervision across the full dataset-size sweep
relationships.reason: Rows r6 and r16 show only limited improvement before an early plateau; Section 4.2.3 explicitly states that increasing data does not resolve OOD generalization.
relationships.display_finding: Performance improved only slightly before an early plateau, and increasing data did not resolve out-of-distribution generalization.

relationships.condition: MPC and LIS direct QA models after their OOD accuracy has plateaued
relationships.reason: For the plateau portion of r6 and r16, Section 4.2.3 explicitly reports no continuing OOD gain despite further data scaling, contradicting continued improvement in this condition.
relationships.display_finding: Further data scaling produced no additional out-of-distribution accuracy gains after the plateau.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The paper says higher-CoT models continue improving OOD accuracy with scale; rows r9–r10 and r19–r20 cover these conditions.
